curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Use a variety of sources to compare the cellular structures of eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, stating the features they share as well as the differences in nucleus, organelles, DNA, size and ribosomes.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Describe the structure and function of the cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplast, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi body, ribosomes, lysosomes and vacuoles in eukaryotic cells

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe the structure and function of each eukaryotic organelle named in the syllabus and trace a protein along the ribosome, ER, Golgi and vesicle pathway.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Contrast the cell structure and organelles of plant and animal cells based on the function of the cell

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can contrast plant and animal cells and justify each difference by the function the cell performs.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Describe the structure and function of the capsule, cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleoid, plasmid, ribosomes, flagella and pili in prokaryotic cells

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe the structure and function of the nine prokaryotic structures named in the syllabus, from the capsule to the pili.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Use calibrated microscope measurements to estimate cell size, including cell size = diameter of field of view ÷ number of cells across the field

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can prepare and observe cells, distinguish a calibrated field-of-view measurement from an image measurement, and calculate real cell size using both methods.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Assess the impact of technological developments in microscopy on scientific understanding of cell structure and function

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can assess how developments from the light microscope to the electron microscope changed scientific understanding of cell structure, weighing strengths against limitations.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Use the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane to explain the structure and function of protein channels, phospholipids, peripheral proteins, integral proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can use the fluid mosaic model to explain the structure and function of phospholipids, protein channels, integral and peripheral proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Explain the processes of simple diffusion, osmosis and facilitated diffusion
Conduct practical investigations to demonstrate the processes of diffusion and osmosis

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain simple diffusion, osmosis and facilitated diffusion as passive processes driven by concentration gradients, and describe practical demonstrations of diffusion and osmosis.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Predict the effects of hypertonic, hypotonic and isotonic solutions on animal and plant cells

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can predict and explain the effects of hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions on animal and plant cells using the direction of osmosis.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Explain the processes of active transport, exocytosis and endocytosis

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis, and say what the ATP is spent on in each.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Relate the movement of glucose, oxygen, carbon dioxide, salts and wastes across membranes to concentration gradients and the characteristics of the materials being exchanged

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can relate how glucose, oxygen, carbon dioxide, salts and wastes cross membranes to their concentration gradients and to their size, polarity and charge.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Relate carbon dioxide, oxygen, water, ions, amino acids and glucose to cell requirements

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can relate carbon dioxide, oxygen, water, ions, amino acids and glucose to the specific requirement each meets, and say when each is an input or an output.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Use the summary equation to describe the process of cellular respiration

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can write the word and balanced summary equations for aerobic respiration and use them to describe the process, including the role of each reactant and product and ATP.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Use the summary equation to describe the process of photosynthesis

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can write the word and balanced summary equations for photosynthesis, identify its reactants, products and energy input, and describe how it complements respiration.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Explain the role of enzymes in cells

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain that enzymes are reusable, specific protein catalysts that lower activation energy, and justify why cells depend on them.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Use diagrams of the induced fit model and the lock and key model to explain the interaction between enzymes and specific substrates

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can use labelled diagrams of the lock-and-key and induced fit models to explain enzyme–substrate specificity and compare the two models.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Plan and conduct laboratory experiments to demonstrate the effect of temperature, pH and substrate concentration on the efficiency of a selected enzyme

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can plan a valid, reliable experiment on one factor affecting catalase, naming the independent, dependent and controlled variables, a control and safety precautions.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Analyse graphs to explain the effect of temperature, pH and substrate concentration on enzyme activity

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can analyse temperature, pH and substrate-concentration graphs, identify the optimum and saturation, and explain each region using collisions, denaturation and saturation.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Use the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) double helix model to demonstrate the structure of DNA, including nucleotide composition, complementary base pairing and hydrogen bonding

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can use the double helix model to describe DNA structure: the three parts of a nucleotide, complementary base pairing (A–T, C–G) and the role of hydrogen bonds.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Conduct a practical investigation to model the process of DNA replication, demonstrating the role of complementary bases, the replication fork with leading and lagging strands, and the enzymes of helicase, primase, DNA polymerases and ligase
Assess the use of models to demonstrate DNA replication

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can model DNA replication, explaining complementary base pairing, the replication fork, leading and lagging strands and the roles of helicase, primase, DNA polymerase and ligase, and assess the model.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Construct diagrams to compare the forms in which DNA exists in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can construct labelled diagrams comparing DNA in prokaryotic cells (circular chromosome, nucleoid, plasmids) and eukaryotic cells (linear chromosomes, histones, nucleus), including what both share.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Compare the structures and roles of somatic and gametic cells

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can compare somatic (diploid, mitosis, growth and repair) and gametic (haploid, meiosis, fertilisation) cells and explain how fertilisation restores the diploid number.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Account for the phases of gap 1 (G1), synthesis, gap 2 (G2) and mitosis in the cell cycle
Conduct a practical investigation to model the named phases of mitosis and cytokinesis

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can account for G1, S, G2 and M in order, model prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase and cytokinesis, and explain why the order produces two identical daughter cells.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Describe the processes of crossing over, independent assortment and random segregation during meiosis
Conduct a practical investigation to model the named phases of meiosis and cytokinesis

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe how meiosis halves the chromosome number and how crossing over, independent assortment and random segregation create genetically different gametes, and model the phases of meiosis.

curriculum.declaredModule: Cells as the basis of life
declaredContentPoints: Evaluate the importance of DNA replication, mitosis, meiosis and cytokinesis in cell division

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can evaluate the importance of DNA replication, mitosis, meiosis and cytokinesis, linking each to its role and to the consequence of its failure, and reach a justified conclusion.

declaredContentPoints: Compare the characteristics and structures of cells in unicellular, colonial and multicellular organisms

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can compare unicellular, colonial and multicellular organisation using cell specialisation, division of labour and interdependence rather than a universal survival-after-separation test.

declaredContentPoints: Explain the effect of the surface-area-to-volume ratio on the rate of movement of materials into and out of a cell
Conduct a laboratory experiment to predict the effect of the surface-area-to-volume ratio on the rate of movement of materials into and out of a cell

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can calculate SA:V for model cubes, explain how SA:V affects the rate of movement of materials into and out of a cell, and predict the result of a diffusion-into-cubes experiment.

declaredContentPoints: Explain the hierarchical organisation of organelles, cells, tissues, organs and systems in organisms

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain the hierarchy from organelle to organism, trace one example up every level, and state what each level can do that the level below cannot.

declaredContentPoints: Describe the nutrient, water and gas requirements of plants for photosynthesis and respiration

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe the gas, water and mineral nutrient requirements of plants and match each to photosynthesis, respiration or both.

declaredContentPoints: Discuss the conditions required for photosynthesis

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can discuss the conditions required for photosynthesis, identify the limiting factor from a graph or scenario, and explain why temperature has an optimum.

declaredContentPoints: Conduct a practical investigation to predict how changes in conditions affect photosynthesis

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can plan a fair test of one condition on the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed, and predict and justify the result using the limiting-factor model.

declaredContentPoints: Use a variety of sources to compare the structures and functions of xylem and phloem in the plant transport system

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can compare the structures and functions of xylem and phloem and link each structural feature to the job it does.

declaredContentPoints: Use the translocation theory to explain the movement of nutrients through phloem tissue

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can use the translocation (pressure-flow) theory to explain how sugar moves through phloem from source to sink, and why the direction can reverse.

declaredContentPoints: Use the cohesion-tension theory to explain how osmotic pressure, transpiration stream and the cohesion of water molecules control the movement of water and dissolved minerals through the xylem

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can use the cohesion-tension theory to explain how osmotic pressure, the transpiration stream and cohesion move water and dissolved minerals up the xylem.

declaredContentPoints: Explain how light, temperature, wind and humidity affect the rate of transpiration in plants

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how light, temperature, wind and humidity each change the rate of transpiration, and reduce all four to stomatal opening and the water-vapour gradient.

declaredContentPoints: Conduct a practical investigation to demonstrate the effect of an environmental factor on the rate of transpiration

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can use a potometer to demonstrate the effect of one environmental factor on transpiration, calculate rates, and evaluate validity, reliability and accuracy.

declaredContentPoints: Conduct a practical investigation to explain the functions of gas exchange, water and nutrient transport in microscopic leaf, stem and root structures

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can prepare and examine sections of leaf, stem and root, and use what they observe to explain gas exchange, water transport and nutrient transport.

declaredContentPoints: Describe the organ systems required for nutrient, water, gas and waste management in animals

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe the organ system that manages each of the four needs (nutrients, water, gases, wastes) and explain how the circulatory system links them to every cell.

declaredContentPoints: Use a variety of sources to describe how the processes of mechanical, physical and chemical digestion, absorption and elimination in the human digestive system enable cellular functions

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe mechanical and chemical digestion, absorption and elimination in order along the tract, and link each to the cellular function it enables.

declaredContentPoints: Account for changes in the concentration of gases, nutrients and wastes in blood as it travels through the lungs, liver, small intestine, large intestine, kidneys and muscles organs in mammals

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can account for the changes in gases, nutrients and wastes in blood leaving the lungs, small intestine, large intestine, liver, kidneys and muscles, using one rule.

declaredContentPoints: Use models to demonstrate the relationship between the structure and function of arteries, capillaries and veins

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can link the structure of arteries, capillaries and veins to their functions, and use a model to demonstrate this while stating its limitations.

declaredContentPoints: Explain the relationship between the structure of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets and their function within blood

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how the structure of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets suits each one's function.

declaredContentPoints: Use models to demonstrate how the organisation of alveoli and capillaries in the lungs allows for efficient gas exchange

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how the organisation of alveoli and capillaries gives a large surface area, a short diffusion distance, a steep gradient and a moist surface, and use a model to demonstrate this.

declaredContentPoints: Explain how glomerular filtration, selective reabsorption and secretion contribute to the removal of waste in nephrons
Use models to explain how the glomerulus, Bowman’s capsule and nephron tubules contribute to filtration and reabsorption for waste removal in the kidney

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how filtration at the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule, and selective reabsorption and secretion in the tubules, together remove waste in a nephron.

declaredContentPoints: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to compare the process of renal dialysis to the function of the kidney

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how haemodialysis cleans the blood, compare it with the kidney using similarities and differences, and judge the reliability of the sources used.

declaredContentPoints: Describe the key components of a typical feedback system, including stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector and response

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe the five components of a feedback system, in order, and map a named example such as getting cold onto them.

declaredContentPoints: Construct and interpret diagrams of negative feedback loops to demonstrate maintenance of homeostasis

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can construct a labelled negative feedback loop for thermoregulation, and interpret it to explain how the response opposes the change in either direction.

declaredContentPoints: Discuss the role of the hypothalamus and pituitary gland in regulating the secretion of hormones

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can discuss how the hypothalamus controls the pituitary, how the pituitary's tropic hormones control target glands, and how negative feedback regulates the chain.

declaredContentPoints: Describe the function of the primary hormones that regulate blood sugar levels and the stress response
Conduct a secondary-source investigation to analyse the impact of diabetes on the body’s ability to maintain homeostasis
Analyse data on hormone levels and physiological processes to illustrate the role of an endocrine hormone in regulating a specific function

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe how insulin, glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol act, analyse paired hormone-and-physiological-response data, and explain how diabetes disrupts glucose homeostasis.

declaredContentPoints: Using a physiological condition discuss the optimal range for functioning and critical tolerance limit

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can use body temperature to distinguish an optimal range from conditions where regulation is stressed or fails, while recognising that critical risk depends on duration, cause and individual factors rather than one universal temperature.

declaredContentPoints: Discuss the role of genetic variation, inheritance and selective pressures in contributing to the process of evolution by natural selection

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain evolution by natural selection as a sequence driven by heritable variation, inheritance and a selective pressure, and say why populations evolve but individuals do not.

declaredContentPoints: Use examples to demonstrate how abiotic and biotic factors exert selective pressures on populations

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can classify a factor as abiotic or biotic and use a named example to show how it selects for a particular heritable trait.

declaredContentPoints: Explain how human-induced changes may function as selective pressures

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how a human activity acts as a selective pressure, identify the trait selected, and distinguish artificial selection from natural selection.

declaredContentPoints: Analyse how evolution causes species diversity

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can analyse how isolation, different selective pressures and reproductive isolation turn one population into separate species, and how repeated speciation builds diversity.

declaredContentPoints: Describe examples from Aboriginal palaeontological evidence that demonstrate the existence of Australian megafauna

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe rock art and oral tradition as Aboriginal palaeontological evidence for Australian megafauna, and explain what each adds to fossil bone.

declaredContentPoints: Evaluate the role of isolation and adaptation in the evolution of Australian monotremes and marsupials

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can evaluate how isolation and adaptation together shaped Australian monotremes and marsupials, using named examples.

declaredContentPoints: Conduct a practical investigation to model the processes involved in natural selection
Discuss the validity of various models that demonstrate natural selection

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can run a predation model of natural selection, process its results as percentages, and discuss the validity of different models of natural selection.

declaredContentPoints: Use examples to explain convergent and divergent evolution

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain convergent and divergent evolution with examples, and use analogous and homologous structures to tell which has occurred.

declaredContentPoints: Use plant and animal examples to explain how structural, physiological and behavioural adaptations shaped by evolution enable survival in their environment

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can classify adaptations as structural, physiological or behavioural and explain, with plant and animal examples, how each enables survival.

declaredContentPoints: Conduct a practical investigation to examine structural adaptations for water balance in Australian plants

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how leaf structures reduce water loss and carry out a fair investigation comparing percentage mass loss between leaves.

declaredContentPoints: Use examples to explain behavioural adaptations used by ectotherms and endotherms to survive in the Australian environment
Analyse data to compare how the external environment and body temperature are related in endotherms and ectotherms

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain behavioural thermoregulation in Australian ectotherms and endotherms and analyse body-temperature data to identify each.

lessons.title: Water and Salt Balance in Aquatic Animals
lessons.subject: Biology

declaredContentPoints: Explain physiological adaptations of aquatic animals to regulate water and salt balance

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can predict the direction of water movement for freshwater and marine animals and explain the physiological adaptations that oppose it.

lessons.title: First Nations Use of Plant & Animal Adaptations
lessons.subject: Biology

declaredContentPoints: Explain how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples use the adaptations of local plants and animals for specific purposes

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples use specific adaptations of local plants and animals for specific purposes, linking each use to the underlying structural, physiological or behavioural adaptation.

declaredContentPoints: Use phylogenetic trees to compare the gradualism model with the punctuated equilibrium model of evolution

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can read a phylogenetic tree and compare the gradualism and punctuated equilibrium models, recognising that both rely on natural selection and common descent and differ only in the rate and timing of change.

declaredContentPoints: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to analyse how human-induced pressures can drive the emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains of bacteria and Dichloro-Diphenyl-Trichloroethane (DDT)-resistant mosquitoes

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain the emergence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria and DDT-resistant mosquitoes as natural selection driven by a human-induced pressure, and analyse and evaluate secondary-source data showing resistance rising.

declaredContentPoints: Analyse information on how transitional fossils, fossil assemblages and relative dating have provided palaeontological and geological evidence for past changes in life forms

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can analyse how transitional fossils, fossil assemblages and relative dating (superposition) provide evidence for past changes in life forms, and state what relative dating can and cannot establish.

declaredContentPoints: Conduct a scientific investigation to infer evolutionary relationships between species using DNA and amino acid sequences

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can align DNA or amino-acid sequences, count and tabulate differences, use a simplified classroom distance comparison to infer relative relatedness, and state the assumptions and limitations without implying that all phylogenetic methods require a strict molecular clock.

declaredContentPoints: Evaluate comparative anatomy, genetic phylogeny, biogeography and biochemistry as evidence for the theory of evolution by natural selection

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can evaluate comparative anatomy, genetic phylogeny, biogeography and biochemistry as evidence for evolution by natural selection, weighing each line's strengths and limitations and reaching a judgement.

declaredContentPoints: Conduct a practical investigation to collect and analyse abiotic and biotic data, to discuss the features of an ecosystem

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can plan and conduct a field investigation that collects abiotic and biotic data, analyse the data, and use it to discuss the features of an ecosystem.

declaredContentPoints: Compare abiotic data from a variety of aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can compare abiotic data across aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems, identify which factors are shared and which are specific, and link the differences to the communities each ecosystem supports.

declaredContentPoints: Explain how abiotic and biotic factors influence the abundance, distribution and diversity of species in an ecosystem

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how abiotic factors (through tolerance ranges and limiting factors) and biotic factors (competition, predation, disease) together influence the abundance, distribution and diversity of species.

declaredContentPoints: Compare sampling techniques to estimate distribution and abundance of organisms
Conduct a practical investigation to examine the distribution and abundance of a plant or animal using belt transect, line transect or quadrat sampling techniques

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can choose between random quadrats, line transects and belt transects, calculate a population estimate or mean percentage cover from quadrat data, and explain how placement and sample size affect reliability.

declaredContentPoints: Conduct a practical investigation to model the mark-release-recapture method and estimate abundance of mobile organisms

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can model mark-release-recapture, calculate a population estimate with the Lincoln index N = (M × C) ÷ R, state its assumptions and predict the direction of error when one is broken.

declaredContentPoints: Use examples to determine relationships between organisms, including predation, competition, mutualism, commensalism, allelopathy and parasitism
Analyse data on the impact of predator–prey relationships and competition on populations

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can classify relationships between organisms by their effect on each partner (+, −, 0), and analyse predator–prey and competition data to explain how these interactions affect populations.

declaredContentPoints: Explain how the carrying capacity of a selected ecosystem is affected by biotic and abiotic factors
Evaluate the validity, reliability and accuracy of ecological sampling data when drawing conclusions about ecosystem dynamics

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain carrying capacity and logistic growth, explain how biotic and abiotic factors set and shift carrying capacity in a selected ecosystem, and evaluate ecological data for validity, reliability and accuracy.

declaredContentPoints: explain the mechanisms of reproduction that ensure the continuity of a species, by analysing sexual and asexual methods of reproduction in a variety of organisms

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how reproduction maintains continuity of a species and compare sexual and asexual reproduction as trade-offs suited to different environments.

declaredContentPoints: model the process of transcription, including the role of the template strand and the formation of mRNA, as part of polypeptide synthesis

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can model transcription, using the template strand and RNA base-pairing to build an mRNA copy of a gene.

declaredContentPoints: model the process of polypeptide synthesis, including translation at the ribosome (ACSBL079)

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can trace a short mRNA sequence through codon-anticodon matching and explain how ribosomes, tRNA and peptide bonds build a polypeptide during translation.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the structure and function of proteins in living things
assess the relationship between the genotype and phenotype, including the effect of the environment

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain the pathway from genotype to phenotype through protein structure and function, and explain how the environment influences phenotype without changing the genotype.

declaredContentPoints: model the formation of new combinations of genotypes produced during meiosis, including crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation
explain how mutation introduces new alleles into a population

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can identify and explain the four sources of genetic variation and distinguish those that create new allele combinations from the one that creates new alleles.

declaredContentPoints: conduct practical investigations to predict variations in the genotype of offspring by modelling meiosis, including crossing over, fertilisation and mutation (ACSBL084)
model the inheritance of autosomal and sex-linked traits using Punnett squares and pedigrees

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can set up Punnett squares for autosomal and X-linked crosses, infer genotypes from pedigrees, and state results as a probability per child.

declaredContentPoints: conduct practical investigations to predict variations in the genotype of offspring by modelling meiosis, fertilisation and mutation (ACSBL084)
investigate inheritance patterns including co-dominance, incomplete dominance and multiple alleles

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can distinguish co-dominance, incomplete dominance and multiple alleles, and use observed phenotype ratios to identify the inheritance pattern.

declaredContentPoints: collect, record and present data to represent frequencies of characteristics in a population, in order to identify trends, patterns, relationships and limitations in data, for example: examining frequency data, analysing single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
Conduct a secondary-source investigation on single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in populations and their association with a genetic disease
Assess potential limitations and constraints of SNP testing and databases in diagnostic medicine

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain what a SNP is, calculate and compare allele frequencies in a case and control sample, explain what a SNP and disease association does and does not show, and assess the limits of SNP testing and databases in diagnosis.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the use of technologies to determine inheritance patterns in a population using, for example: DNA sequencing and profiling (ACSBL064, ACSBL085)
Use examples to explain how biotechnologies diagnose genetic diseases
Discuss the roles of biological knowledge, genetic engineering and bioinformatics techniques used in biotechnology

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how DNA sequencing and bioinformatics are used to diagnose genetic diseases such as cystic fibrosis, alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency and Leber congenital amaurosis, and distinguish sequencing from DNA profiling by what each produces.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the use of data analysis from a large-scale collaborative project to identify trends, patterns and relationships, for example: the use of population genetics data in conservation management, population genetics studies used to determine the inheritance of a disease or disorder (ACSBL064, ACSBL073)
Assess the use of genetic databases for the analysis of the prevalence of a genetic disease
Assess the role of data and modelling in developing and using biotechnology
Explain how the founder effect and bottlenecks result in genetic drift
Analyse data on the effect of reduced genetic diversity on the survival of Tasmanian devil populations

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how shared genetic databases such as GenBank and EMBL are built and used, model the prevalence of cystic fibrosis carriers with the Hardy Weinberg equation, assess what databases can and cannot show about prevalence, and explain how population genetic data guides Tasmanian devil conservation.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the use of data analysis from a large-scale collaborative project to identify trends, patterns and relationships, for example: population genetics studies used to determine the inheritance of a disease or disorder (ACSBL064, ACSBL073)
Discuss the risks and benefits of using biotechnologies to provide personalised information about the risk of developing, and management of, a non-infectious disease
Assess potential limitations and constraints of SNP testing and databases in diagnostic medicine

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain why population genetic data predicts group trends better than individual outcomes, describe how single gene tests and polygenic risk scores give personalised risk information for non-infectious diseases, and discuss the benefits and risks of that information.

declaredContentPoints: analyse sexual and asexual methods of reproduction in animals, including internal and external fertilisation

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain how fertilisation restores the diploid number and compare external and internal fertilisation as strategies shaped by environment.

lessons.title: Reproduction in Plants, Fungi, Bacteria and Protists
lessons.subject: Biology

declaredContentPoints: analyse sexual and asexual methods of reproduction in plants, fungi, bacteria and protists, including the role of pollination and vegetative propagation

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can distinguish pollination from fertilisation and compare the sexual and asexual reproductive strategies of plants, fungi, bacteria and protists.

declaredContentPoints: describe the events of fertilisation, implantation, pregnancy and birth in mammals, including the role of hormones

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can sequence the events from fertilisation to birth in mammals and explain how hormones and the placenta sustain pregnancy.

curriculum.declaredModule: Module 5 Heredity and Module 6 Genetic Change (2017) + Biotechnology and Biodiversity (2025)
declaredContentPoints: evaluate the impact of scientific knowledge on the manipulation of plant and animal reproduction in agriculture (ACSBL074)
compare the processes and outcomes of reproductive technologies, including but not limited to: artificial insemination, artificial pollination
Account for the use of artificial pollination in Australian agriculture, including its methods and outcomes
Compare germline genetic changes in reproductive and genetic engineering biotechnologies
Explain impacts of monoculture, pesticide use, land clearing and habitat loss on the health of ecosystems

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe the methods and outcomes of artificial pollination in Australian agriculture, explain how reproductive technologies such as artificial insemination change what is inherited, and compare those germline changes with genetic engineering.

curriculum.declaredModule: Module 5 Heredity (2017) + Cells as the basis of life (2025)
declaredContentPoints: DNA replication using the Watson and Crick DNA model, including nucleotide composition, pairing and bonding (ACSBL076, ACSBL077)
Use the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) double helix model to demonstrate the structure of DNA, including nucleotide composition, complementary base pairing and hydrogen bonding

Conduct a practical investigation to model the process of DNA replication, demonstrating the role of complementary bases, the replication fork with leading and lagging strands, and the enzymes of helicase, primase, DNA polymerases and ligase
Assess the use of models to demonstrate DNA replication

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe DNA structure, explain semiconservative replication, and name the roles of helicase, primase, DNA polymerases and ligase at a replication fork with leading and lagging strands.

curriculum.declaredModule: Module 5 Heredity (2017) + Cells as the basis of life (2025)
declaredContentPoints: model the processes involved in cell replication, including but not limited to: mitosis and meiosis (ACSBL075)
assess the effect of the cell replication processes on the continuity of species (ACSBL084)
Account for the phases of gap 1 (G1), synthesis, gap 2 (G2) and mitosis in the cell cycle
Compare the structures and roles of somatic and gametic cells
Conduct a practical investigation to model the named phases of mitosis and cytokinesis

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can account for the G1, S, G2 and M phases of the cell cycle, sequence mitosis and cytokinesis, compare somatic and gametic cells, and explain how mitosis maintains chromosome number.

declaredContentPoints: model the process of meiosis, including reduction division, crossing over and independent assortment, and explain its role in sexual reproduction and variation

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can model meiosis as a reduction division and explain how crossing over and independent assortment generate variation while keeping chromosome number stable across generations.

declaredContentPoints: compare the structure and organisation of DNA in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, including the role of plasmids and chromosomes

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can compare how DNA is structured and organised in prokaryotes and eukaryotes and explain why that organisation matters for biotechnology.

declaredContentPoints: compare the causes, processes and effects of different types of mutation, including but not limited to point and chromosomal mutation
investigate the causes of genetic variation relating to the processes of fertilisation, meiosis and mutation (ACSBL078)

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain that mutation is the source of new alleles, while meiosis and fertilisation only reshuffle alleles that already exist.

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can name straight-chain and branched alkanes, alkenes and alkynes up to C8 using IUPAC rules, and state the shape and bond angle at any carbon from its bond type.

lessons.title: Production of Alcohols: Hydration, Substitution, Fermentation
lessons.subject: Chemistry

declaredContentPoints: investigate the production of alcohols, including:
write equations, state conditions and predict products to represent the reactions of alcohols, including but not limited to (ACSCH128, ACSCH136):

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can write equations and conditions for producing alcohols by hydration, haloalkane substitution and fermentation, and compare the methods.

lessons.title: Combustion of Alcohols & Comparison with Fossil Fuels
lessons.subject: Chemistry

declaredContentPoints: conduct a practical investigation to measure and reliably compare the enthalpy of combustion for a range of alcohols
compare and contrast fuels from organic sources to biofuels, including ethanol

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can calculate molar enthalpy of combustion from calorimetry data, explain why experimental values are systematically low, and describe the energy trend down the alcohol series.

lessons.title: Reactions of Alcohols: Dehydration, Substitution, Oxidation
lessons.subject: Chemistry

declaredContentPoints: write equations, state conditions and predict products to represent the reactions of alcohols, including but not limited to (ACSCH128, ACSCH136):
investigate the products of the oxidation of primary and secondary alcohols

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can write equations and conditions for dehydration, HX substitution and oxidation of alcohols, and predict oxidation products from the alcohol class.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the products of the oxidation of primary and secondary alcohols
investigate the structural formulae, properties and functional group including: primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, aldehydes and ketones

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can distinguish aldehydes from ketones by structure, name them, predict their relative boiling points, and identify them using Tollens' and Fehling's tests.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the structural formulae, properties and functional group including: carboxylic acids
explain the properties within and between the homologous series of carboxylic acids, amines and amides with reference to the intermolecular and intramolecular bonding present

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain the anomalously high boiling points of carboxylic acids via dimerisation, write equations for their reactions as weak acids, and use the sodium hydrogen carbonate test to identify them.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the production, in a school laboratory, of simple esters
investigate the structural formulae, properties and functional group including: esters

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can name esters as alkyl alkanoates, write reversible esterification equations with the correct catalyst and conditions, and apply Le Chatelier's principle to raise the yield.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the structural formulae, properties and functional group including: amines and amides
explain the properties within and between the homologous series of carboxylic acids, amines and amides with reference to the intermolecular and intramolecular bonding present

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can classify amines, explain their basicity and that of amides using the nitrogen lone pair, write amine reactions with acids, and rank boiling points across the families.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the structure and action of soaps and detergents
investigate the production, in a school laboratory, of soap

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe soap's amphipathic structure and micelle cleaning action, write saponification equations, and compare soaps with synthetic detergents in hard water.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the differences between an organic acid and organic base
explain the properties within and between the homologous series of carboxylic acids, amines and amides with reference to the intermolecular and intramolecular bonding present

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can rank organic acid strength using pKa and conjugate-base stability, explain the inductive effect, and design a reagent scheme to distinguish acid classes.

declaredContentPoints: write equations, state conditions and predict products to represent the reactions of alcohols
investigate the products of organic reactions including but not limited to: addition, substitution, oxidation, esterification and combustion reactions

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can use the functional-group reaction map to plan a multi-step synthesis, choosing the correct reagents and conditions and avoiding dead ends.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature II: Functional Groups & Isomers
lessons.subject: Chemistry

declaredContentPoints: investigate the nomenclature of organic chemicals, up to C8, using IUPAC conventions, including simple methyl and ethyl branched chains, including: (ACSCH127)
explore and distinguish the different types of structural isomers, including saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons, including: (ACSCH035)

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can name compounds across the eight functional group classes and classify a pair of structural isomers as chain, position or functional group isomers.

declaredContentPoints: write equations, state conditions and predict products to represent the reactions of hydrocarbons and alcohols
investigate the products of organic reactions including but not limited to: addition, substitution, oxidation, esterification and combustion reactions

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can recall every Module 7 reaction with exact conditions, avoid the most-penalised omissions, and structure a full-mark multi-step pathway response.

declaredContentPoints: model and compare the structure, properties and uses of addition polymers of ethylene and related monomers

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe addition polymerisation, draw repeat units and monomers, and explain how chain branching and side groups control polymer properties.

declaredContentPoints: model and compare the structure, properties and uses of condensation polymers, for example: nylon and polyesters

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe condensation polymerisation, identify the monomers and linkages of PET and nylon, and contrast condensation with addition polymerisation.

declaredContentPoints: model and compare the structure, properties and uses of addition polymers of ethylene and related monomers
model and compare the structure, properties and uses of condensation polymers, for example: nylon and polyesters

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can link polymer chain structure to bulk properties, distinguish thermoplastics from thermosets, justify polymer choices, and evaluate environmental impact.

declaredContentPoints: construct models, identify the functional group, and write structural and molecular formulae for homologous series of organic chemical compounds, up to C8 (ACSCH035)
conduct an investigation to compare the properties of organic chemical compounds within a homologous series, and explain these differences in terms of bonding (ACSCH035)
explain the properties within and between the homologous series of alkanes with reference to the intermolecular and intramolecular bonding present

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain boiling point and solubility trends across hydrocarbons using dispersion forces, surface area and the disrupt-and-replace model.

declaredContentPoints: analyse the shape of molecules formed between carbon atoms when a single, double or triple bond is formed between them
construct models, identify the functional group, and write structural and molecular formulae for homologous series of organic chemical compounds, up to C8 (ACSCH035)

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe the shape and bond angle at single, double and triple bonded carbons, and explain why the pi bond makes alkenes and alkynes reactive.

declaredContentPoints: investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of unsaturated hydrocarbons when added to a range of chemicals, including but not limited to:
investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of saturated hydrocarbons when substituted with halogens

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can classify a hydrocarbon reaction as combustion, substitution, addition or polymerisation, and write a balanced equation for each.

lessons.title: Reactions of Alkenes: Addition & Markovnikov's Rule
lessons.subject: Chemistry

declaredContentPoints: investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of unsaturated hydrocarbons when added to a range of chemicals, including but not limited to:

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can write equations with full conditions for the four alkene addition reactions and apply Markovnikov's rule to choose the major product.

declaredContentPoints: investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of unsaturated hydrocarbons when added to a range of chemicals, including but not limited to:
investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of saturated hydrocarbons when substituted with halogens

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can write two-step alkyne additions, explain why alkyne hydration gives a ketone, and state correctly that UV light is the energy source for alkane substitution.

lessons.title: Hydrocarbon Reactions Mastery: Conditions, Products & Errors
lessons.subject: Chemistry

declaredContentPoints: investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of unsaturated hydrocarbons when added to a range of chemicals, including but not limited to:
investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of saturated hydrocarbons when substituted with halogens

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can reproduce the full conditions for every hydrocarbon reaction, plan multi-step syntheses, and spot and fix wrong conditions, products and reaction types.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the structural formulae, properties and functional group including:
explain the properties within and between the homologous series of alcohols with reference to the intermolecular and intramolecular bonding present

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can classify alcohols as primary, secondary or tertiary and explain their boiling points and solubility using hydrogen bonding and dispersion forces.

declaredContentPoints: conduct practical investigations to analyse the concentration of an unknown acid or base by titration
investigate the use of indicators and pH to determine the equivalence point of acid-base reactions

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can average concordant titres, run the four-step mole pathway for any ratio, choose an indicator from the equivalence pH, and solve a back titration by subtracting the excess.

declaredContentPoints: analyse the need for monitoring the environment
investigate the chemistry involved in the maintenance of water quality in a chosen body of water

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe each stage of the drinking-water treatment train by its chemical purpose and explain why HOCl is the active disinfecting species.

declaredContentPoints: conduct qualitative investigations to test for the presence in organic molecules of the following functional groups: carboxylic acids, amines, amides
investigate the structure and action of named medicines in terms of their functional groups

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can classify medicines by function and structure, identify the key functional groups in common drugs, and explain the pharmacophore concept.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the structure and action of named medicines in terms of their functional groups
explore the relationship between the structure of a drug and its acid-base behaviour

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can apply the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation to find the ionised-to-unionised ratio of a weak-acid drug and explain how pH controls absorption.

lessons.title: Optical Isomerism and Chirality in Medicines
lessons.subject: Chemistry

declaredContentPoints: investigate the processes used to analyse the structure of simple organic compounds addressed in the course
examine the structural formulae and properties of optical isomers (enantiomers) and their significance in medicine

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can identify a chiral centre, distinguish enantiomers from other isomers, and explain why chiral biology makes enantiopurity matter, using thalidomide.

declaredContentPoints: investigate the structure and action of named medicines in terms of their functional groups
relate the polarity and solubility of a drug to its absorption and method of delivery

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can apply like-dissolves-like and Lipinski's rule to drug solubility, and match a delivery route to a solubility or first-pass metabolism problem.

declaredContentPoints: evaluate the factors that need to be considered when designing a chemical synthesis process, including but not limited to: availability of reagents, reaction conditions, yield and purity, industrial uses, environmental, social and economic issues
assess the sustainability of a chemical synthesis using atom economy and other green chemistry principles

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can describe the aspirin synthesis, calculate atom economy and E-factor, and evaluate a route's sustainability beyond yield alone.

declaredContentPoints: model and compare the structure, properties and uses of addition polymers of ethylene and related monomers
model and compare the structure, properties and uses of condensation polymers

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can distinguish addition from condensation polymers and link chain length, branching, cross-linking and intermolecular forces to polymer properties.

declaredContentPoints: conduct investigations and/or process data involving the gravimetric analysis of a sample to determine the percentage by mass of an analyte

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can run the precipitate-to-analyte mole pathway, calculate percentage by mass, and state the direction each procedural error pushes the result.

declaredContentPoints: conduct qualitative investigations using flame tests, precipitation and complexation reactions to test for the presence of ions in aqueous solution
use precipitation and net ionic equations to identify ions present in a sample

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can identify cations and anions from characteristic precipitates, gases and flame colours, write net ionic equations, and treat single tests as evidence rather than proof.

declaredContentPoints: conduct investigations and/or process data to determine the concentration of coloured species and/or metal ions using colourimetry or UV-visible spectrophotometry, and atomic absorption spectroscopy

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can apply the Beer-Lambert law, read an unknown from a calibration curve, explain that AAS measures ground-state atoms after atomisation, and choose between UV-Vis and AAS for a task.

declaredContentPoints: conduct investigations and/or process data involving chromatographic techniques to separate and identify the components of a mixture
calculate Rf values and interpret chromatographic data to identify components and assess purity

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain separation by differential affinity, calculate and interpret Rf, choose between TLC, column and HPLC, and read a chromatogram for identity and purity.

declaredContentPoints: analyse the need for monitoring the environment
investigate the chemical analysis of water quality parameters and compare measured values against acceptable standards

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can classify water-quality parameters, link each to its measurement method, judge values against standards like the ADWG, and trace the eutrophication chain.

declaredContentPoints: analyse the need for monitoring the environment
conduct investigations and/or process data to measure dissolved oxygen and biochemical oxygen demand in water samples

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can explain the Winkler chain, use the 1:4 oxygen-to-thiosulfate ratio to find DO, calculate BOD₅, and read DO and BOD together to judge a waterway.

declaredContentPoints: conduct investigations and/or process data to determine the concentration of heavy metal ions in aqueous solution using atomic absorption spectroscopy
analyse the need for monitoring the environment for heavy metal contamination

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can name key heavy metals and sources, justify AAS for trace monitoring, distinguish bioaccumulation from biomagnification, and match remediation strategies to context.

declaredContentPoints: analyse the need for monitoring the environment
conduct investigations to analyse the concentration of an appropriate range of ions in a local body of water

teaching.declaredIntent: Students can trace the eutrophication sequence from nutrient loading to fish kill and identify the analytical methods used to monitor nitrate and phosphate.
